hook: The goldsmith of Mainz whose printing press changed the world.

pages.x: Johannes Gutenberg was born around 1400 in Mainz, in Germany, and trained in metalwork. Forced out by a quarrel in the city, he moved to Strasbourg, where he made little mirrors for pilgrims, which were said to catch the holy power of relics.
He brought together metal letters cast in a hand mould, an oily ink, and a press like a wine press, so pages could be printed fast and the letters used again and again.
pages.fx: A press could print thousands of pages a day, where a scribe copied a few. In 50 years some 20 million books were printed in Europe.

pages.x: Around 1455 in Mainz he printed about 180 copies of the Bible in Latin, each of 1,282 pages, so beautiful they looked handwritten. Forty-nine survive, and a single copy is worth tens of millions of dollars.

He had borrowed heavily from a lawyer, Johann Fust, who sued him just as the Bible was nearly done and took over his workshop and type. Gutenberg ended his days on a small pension from the archbishop of Mainz, paid in grain, wine and clothes.

Printing spread like wildfire. By 1500 there were presses in more than 250 towns, and printed books carried the Renaissance, the Reformation and the new science across Europe. Martin Luther called printing "God's highest act of grace".
pages.img: Global spread of the printing press

pages.x: Gutenberg's press is often called the most important invention of the last thousand years. Cheap books spread ideas faster than any ruler could stop them, and made the Reformation, modern science and mass reading possible.
pts: Brought printing with movable metal type to Europe
